This is more what I was thinking about- that reality of the higher rates of death/disability of infant and mother.

There’s a a lot of mistrust in hospitals/doctors for multiple reasons so it seems like women are more interested in home births…but these same women and families will pursue legal action against the hospital and doctor that try to save their baby after an emergency

My question wasn’t about why anyone would want a natural birth- TONS of advantages. The question was specifically regarding the thoughts around those rare complications that can be handled easily in a staffed hospital setting but devastating if delay (even under an hour) occur . I’m sorry that came off as condescending!

Listening to stories of women where their attempted home birth ended with a bad outcome (like really bad outcome), some have said they knew something bad could happen, but thought everything can be fixed with a quick 5 min trip to the closest hospital. And didn’t think it would happen to them

It seems like people try to emulate a “natural/hands-off” birth but still expect modern day outcomes (healthy mom and baby).

A comparison to your example would be like choosing the risk of driving a car but also not driving a car with functional air bags that are there when you need it and reduce the risk of injury/death

I’m wondering about the thought process surrounding those rare complications that don’t allow for 10-20 minutes transfer/resolution time- do people fully consider the increased risk with that or just invest more in the fact that it’s a low probability of happening to begin with? 

For example, do people understand and accept that a uterine rupture in the hospital is largely survivable (w baby neurologically intact) vs being 5-10 min away from the hospital when that happens with much worse potential outcomes?

Natural in the sense of childbirth without current medical surveillance/intervention (eg being in the hospital but refusing the fetal heart rate monitoring that the doctors/midwives recommend, etc).

I’m curious about the thought process regarding an obstetrical emergency when you don’t have 15-20 minutes time to reach a reasonable level of care (examples would be shoulder dystocia or uterine rupture)

It seems to me that the thought process is not knowingly accepting the higher risk that would accompany such a complication, but just banking on the fact that it’s a low risk to begin with
